extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty, department chairs, teaching committees, and graduate student instructors involved in evaluating or improving undergraduate mathematics teaching
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for evaluating and improving undergraduate mathematics teaching at the department level, including use of student opinion surveys, peer visits, videotaped feedback, and revisions to merit/renewal procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault: survey items presume teacher-as-presenter image
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the items in the survey were written from the perspective that an effective teacher is essentially a presenter and an authority figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing student survey items that presuppose a model of teaching as lecture-and-authority; instead align items with current standards of effective teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault: student opinions can be inconsistent with other measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The student opinions were not entirely consistent with other measures of teaching effectiveness. For example, some faculty found they could improve their student evaluation ratings by doing things they did not consider to be effective practice or by ceasing to do things that they believed were good instructional practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use student opinions as one input among others; be wary of incentivizing practices that raise ratings but reduce instructional quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault: label student data as opinion, not evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty objected to calling the data collected from students 'evaluations' but did not object to it being called 'opinions,' since the data were to be input to an evaluation performed by faculty members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to student-provided data as 'student opinion' or 'student satisfaction' rather than as the sole 'student evaluation' of teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault: mandate to collect student data is not mandate on its weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regents had mandated the use of student evaluation data but had not mandated that it represent the preponderance of evidence of effective teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the intended role and weight of student opinion within overall faculty evaluation policies; do not assume mandated collection implies dominant weight in decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault: comparing single numerical scores misleads
rubrics_metrics.description: We had been led to evaluate teaching effectiveness by comparing single numerical scores... each score was translated into a decile... What started out as a fairly good evaluation (between average and good) was ultimately translated into a rating which suggested poor showing (since you were in the bottom fifth of all teachers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing complex student-opinion data to a single departmental percentile or decile without context; be careful interpreting averaged scores across courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: collect student opinions systematically and label them correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinions of students should be collected systematically as input to an evaluation of teaching to be made by faculty. The input should be properly referred to as 'student opinion' or as 'student satisfaction' and not be referred to as 'student evaluation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish systematic collection procedures and clear terminology to frame student data as input rather than definitive evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: survey items should elicit observable classroom behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The survey instrument should, as much as possible, ask students to record observations of what they perceive in the classroom; it should not ask for direct evaluative judgment on those observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design survey prompts that ask 'what did you observe?' (e.g. frequency of a behavior) rather than 'rate quality' whenever feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: faculty ownership of survey items
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty should have 'ownership' of the items in the survey instrument, by selecting them from a larger bank of items or by constructing them to match with teaching standards they have adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage faculty in selecting or constructing the survey items so items align with departmental teaching standards and increase buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: recognize limits of student input for non-observable tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Student opinions most often reflect classroom performance. Classroom performance is one aspect of teaching effectiveness. Other very important aspects are curriculum planning, materials development and assessment. Generally, students are not reliable sources for input into evaluating those components of effective teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement student opinion with peer review and documentation for out-of-class activities such as curriculum development, assessment design, and professional growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation: faculty involvement in a program of improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every faculty member should be involved, perhaps with a group of others in the department, in a program of improvement. That program can and, perhaps, should include making visits to classes of colleagues and having colleagues visit their classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require or encourage faculty participation in collaborative improvement programs including mutual class visits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation: faculty involvement in assessment of students, courses, and programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Every faculty member should be involved in the assessment of students, courses and programs and in the formulation of reasonable strategies for improving those students, courses and programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document faculty contributions to assessment activities and improvement strategies as part of teaching effectiveness evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation: faculty involvement in curriculum building
rubrics_metrics.description: Every faculty member should be involved in curriculum building by designing new courses, revising old courses, and constructing meaningful activities for students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider curriculum development activities as a component of teaching performance and include evidence in review dossiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation: faculty should collect and use student opinions for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every faculty member should collect student opinions of his/her teaching and should consider those opinions as part of a program for improving his/her teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require routine collection of student opinion and reflective use of that data in improvement plans or statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit reform: use observable expectations and a five-point scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than have the committee rate each individual on a scale of 1–9, the department would develop a statement of what is expected and the committee would rate faculty on a five point scale with 'meets expectations' in the middle. The expectation would be stated in observable terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define expectations in observable language and use a consistent five-point rating scale centered on 'meets expectations' to reduce arbitrariness and align with renewal/promotion formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit reform: focus on improvement and improvement plans
rubrics_metrics.description: The old policy did not promote improvement in teaching... With the 'expectations' approach we can ask for evidence that the instructor has thought about teaching, has done some honest reflection on teaching, and has a realistic plan for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require reflective statements and concrete improvement plans as part of merit review evidence; reward documented professional development efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit reform: connect individual evaluation to department assessment responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The old policy did not promote improvement in programs offered by the department... A revised merit policy should recognize individual efforts that help the department meet its collective responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and recognize contributions that support program-level assessment and improvement when evaluating individual faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit reform: student opinions as input, not direct merit points
rubrics_metrics.description: We have taken steps to reduce the amount of weight given to student opinions. In fact student opinions will not factor directly into merit points in the future. Rather, student opinion is one of several factors that are considered by the Renewal Committee or the Post Tenure Review Committee as they make an evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat student opinion as one of multiple evidence streams; do not convert student scores directly into merit points without committee contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit reform: broaden definition of teaching to include out-of-class tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: We have broadened the definition of effective teaching to include performance on tasks that usually take place outside of the classroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include curriculum planning, materials development, assessment design, and other out-of-class professional activities in teaching evaluation rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 1: use of class time
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. This teacher makes _____ use of class time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - very good; 4 - good; 3 - satisfactory; 2 - poor; 1 - very poor. Use as observable student-reported measure of time management.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 2: syllabus explains course requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: 2. The syllabus (course outline) did _____ job in explaining course requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - a very good; 4 - a good; 3 - an adequate; 2 - not do an adequate; 1 - (there is no syllabus/course outline). Use to measure clarity and availability of course expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 3: raises thought-provoking ideas / asks challenging questions
rubrics_metrics.description: 3. This teacher raises thought-provoking ideas and asks challenging questions _____ during most class periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - several times; 4 - more than a few times; 3 - a few times; 2 - one or two times; 1 - zero times. Use as an observable indicator of cognitive challenge and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 4: provides feedback on progress
rubrics_metrics.description: 4. This teacher provides _____ feedback on my progress in the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - a great deal of; 4 - more than an average amount of; 3 - an average amount of; 2 - little; 1 - very little or no. Use to assess frequency/quality of feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 5: assignments used as learning tools
rubrics_metrics.description: 5. The assignments (papers, performances, projects, exams, etc.) in this class are _____ used as learning tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - always; 4 - almost always; 3 - sometimes; 2 - seldom; 1 - never. Use to gauge pedagogical alignment of assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 6: tests assess understanding vs memorization
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. Tests _____ assess knowledge of facts and understanding of concepts instead of memorization of trivial details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - always; 4 - almost always; 3 - usually; 2 - often do not; 1 - almost never. Use to measure assessment quality from student perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 7: teaching gives opportunity to gain factual knowledge and principles
rubrics_metrics.description: 7. The quality of teaching in this course is giving me _____ opportunity to gain factual knowledge and important principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - a very good; 4 - a good; 3 - an average; 2 - a poor; 1 - a very poor. Use to assess perceived learning value.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 8: teacher attentive and considerate listening to students
rubrics_metrics.description: 8. This teacher is _____ attentive and considerate when listening to students’ questions and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - always; 4 - almost always; 3 - usually; 2 - often not; 1 - never or almost never. Use to measure instructor responsiveness and rapport.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 9: work assigned contributes to understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: 9. The work assigned contributes _____ to my understanding of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - a very significant amount; 4 - a significant amount; 3 - a good amount; 2 - little; 1 - very little. Use to assess alignment of assignments to learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS item 10: course difficulty level challenging
rubrics_metrics.description: 10. The difficulty level of this course is _____ challenging to me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale: 5 - constantly; 4 - often; 3 - sometimes; 2 - almost never; 1 - never. Use to understand perceived challenge level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer observation program: pair junior and senior faculty for exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Every semester, each junior faculty member is paired with a senior member to exchange class visits. The department chair arranges pairs so that over the course of a few years, every senior colleague observes each junior colleague. The chair also insures that someone observes every course taught by a junior colleague at least once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic pairing and rotation to ensure broad exposure and that each junior faculty member is observed at least once per course; consider special requests for particular courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer visits (senior→junior): formal structure and context-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because visits to classes are part of the department’s evaluation of junior faculty, they follow a formal structure under college guidelines. Early in the semester the two faculty members meet and go over the course syllabus. Two or sometimes three consecutive classes are visited. In the discussion following a visit, it is important to put observations into context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require pre-visit syllabus review, observe multiple consecutive class meetings when possible, and hold contextualizing post-visit discussions before finalizing written evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer visits (junior→senior): informal, non-evaluative visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Visits by junior faculty to senior faculty classes are less structured... Unlike senior visits to junior classes, they are not evaluative. Because these visits are not a formal part of departmental evaluation procedures, sometimes they don’t even take place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage but do not require junior visits to senior classes; treat them as professional-development observations rather than evaluative events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-visit write-up content requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The write-up includes a general description of the class, specific comments both positive and negative, and the suggestions or ideas discussed after the visit. The senior colleague then conveys [this] to the junior colleague in writing, with a copy to the department chair. This letter becomes part of the junior faculty member’s file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize write-ups to include context, concrete observations, balanced positives/negatives, and suggested improvements; save copies in personnel files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer observation benefit: visitor sees student reactions and subtle effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A visitor in the back of the room can watch student reactions to various aspects of the class in a way the teacher running the class may not be able to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage observer vantage to capture student engagement patterns and nonverbal cues that the instructor may miss; include these observations in feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video+peer program: combine classroom discussions, peer observation, and videotaped consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: The training program relied essentially on three methods: the program’s classroom discussions, peer observation and criticism, and a video consultation session with the Teaching Consultant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure improvement programs around discussion, reciprocal peer observation, and guided video review rather than relying on a single method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video consultation: guided self-analysis with an experienced Teaching Consultant
rubrics_metrics.description: Twice during the semester, GSIs, while teaching their classes, were videotaped... This video was the basis of an intensive evaluation and consultation session with the Teaching Consultant. First the novice GSI and the Consultant watched the video alone... Then, while watching the video together, the Teaching Consultant led the GSI through a sort of guided self-analysis of his or her performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use videotape review sessions led by an experienced consultant to guide instructor self-analysis, focusing on teaching behaviors rather than production values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video use: augment live observations, not replace them
rubrics_metrics.description: Use videos only to augment actual observations, and have the Teaching Consultant make the video while observing the class. Because a videotape only imperfectly records what went on in the classroom... one should never evaluate a teacher using a videotape of a class one didn’t attend. Rather, use videos to augment actual observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always pair videotape review with direct observation notes from the same observer; avoid basing high-stakes evaluations solely on videotape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video logistics: have consultant set up and occasionally check camera
rubrics_metrics.description: We found it very convenient for the Teaching Consultant to simply arrive a few minutes early to set up equipment, and then occasionally check the camera during the class while taking notes and recording points to be discussed later in the consultation session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign an informed observer to operate and monitor recording equipment so the tape captures relevant boardwork and classroom interaction rather than cinematic close-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not show videos as part of discussion sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not show the videos as a part of the discussion session. In previous years, a large part of program consisted of viewing videos. But this is a waste of time. It is far better to simply send the GSIs into each other’s classrooms and then discuss the issues that arise in the GSI discussion section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer live peer observations combined with discussion over group video-viewing during class meetings; use video selectively in one-on-one consultations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mini-teaching or simulated teaching exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mini-teaching sessions or other forms of simulated teaching. Important parts of teaching well... simply cannot be simulated; there is no substitute for actual students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize real-classroom observations over contrived simulations; use simulation only for very focused technique practice when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Videotape instructors more than once
rubrics_metrics.description: Videotape the GSIs twice. Once is not enough. The first time one sees oneself on videotape is a bit disconcerting... With a second tape, it is much easier to focus on the teaching. Also, taping twice may show improvements in the instructor’s teaching effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule at least two taped teaching sessions to allow instructors to acclimate and to provide evidence of improvement over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage experienced faculty participation in peer/video programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage experienced GSIs and professors to participate in the video consultation program. Experienced faculty can benefit from the critical feedback which lies at the heart of our program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include experienced teachers in peer-observation and consultation schedules to model practices and broaden benefits beyond novices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer observation: have each observer observe many colleagues
rubrics_metrics.description: Let each GSI observe and evaluate many other GSIs. This was one of the most effective and easy-to-organize means of giving a lot of diverse criticism to each GSI, and, simultaneously, expose each GSI to various teaching styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize observation rotations so each instructor both observes multiple colleagues and is observed by multiple peers to gain diverse perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational recommendation: insist on a rigorous schedule for consultation sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Insist on a rigorous schedule for the consultation sessions. We had problems scheduling all the sessions and would have benefitted from a rigorous initial policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish firm scheduling policies and monitor compliance to ensure all consultations occur as planned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success factor: focus on improving teaching rather than rewards/punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus as much as possible on improving teaching and as little as possible on rewards and punishments. Faculty can be motivated to participate in a program of professional development much more readily than they can be persuaded to participate in a system designed to reward or punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluation systems to foster professional growth (coaching, development) rather than zero-sum ranking and punitive incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success factor: build consensus on explicit teaching standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus as much as possible on developing and building consensus for your own statement of standards of teaching as a foundation for evaluating teaching. Evaluation should be based on an explicit standard, a standard with which all faculty can identify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop department-specific standards through faculty consensus and use them as the baseline for evaluations and survey item selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success factor: extend definition of teaching beyond classroom performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on a definition of teaching that extends to tasks that are performed outside the classroom. Teaching effectiveness is much more than a 'performance' in the classroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include curricular work, assessment design, mentoring, and program-level activities in standards and evidence portfolios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success factor: determine a realistic role for student input
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a realistic role for student input. Determine the role that you want student data to play in the evaluation process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly define and document how student opinion will be used (e.g., formative feedback, one evidence stream among many) to avoid misinterpretation and misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success factor: expect incremental solutions and continue seeking improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not expect anything more than temporary, partial solutions but continue to seek more permanent and complete solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reforms as iterative; monitor outcomes and refine instruments and policies over time rather than expecting an immediate perfect system.
